blocks.text: Optimizations should protect the render pipeline and reduce playback stalls. The deep dive here is about controlling network, CPU, and memory while keeping playback instant.

blocks.title: Frontend performance strategies
items: Preconnect to CDN and warm the first media request.
Prefetch next N videos during idle time; cancel on rapid scroll.
Virtualize offscreen items and keep DOM size bounded.
Pause/stop playback when cards exit the viewport.
Use low-res posters and upgrade when stable.
Throttle scroll-driven state updates to avoid re-render storms.

blocks.title: Playback reliability
items: Choose a conservative MP4 rendition before playback from measured session evidence.
On a later attempt, choose a lower rendition or remain poster-only when recovery is unlikely.
Abort in-flight requests when the user skips quickly.
Capture errors with a retry UI and silent auto-retry.

blocks.title: Unreliable shortcut
blocks.text: Vague answers like “use CDN” without showing how prefetching, cancellation, and playback lifecycle actually work on the client.

blocks.title: Keeping swipes smooth while media work changes

steps.title: 1) Batch updates
steps.text: Coalesce viewport and progress presentation only when profiling shows excess commits; playback and user intent still update immediately.

steps.title: 2) Bound the DOM
steps.text: Virtualize offscreen video cards while retaining stable item and scroll-anchor identity.

steps.title: 3) Cancel stale work
steps.text: Abort prefetches or network work when user intent changes.

steps.title: 4) Measure
steps.text: Log LCP/INP and feature-specific KPIs to validate rollout.

blocks.title: Failure modes
rows: Show an explicit play control and keep the card focused.
The UI never claims playback started.
Keep poster and controls visible with retry or lower-quality choice.
Quarantine that candidate and try a compatible fallback.
One broken item does not stop the feed.
Pause visual work and apply a clear playback policy.
Return does not start multiple players.

blocks.text: Cards expose a stable heading, playback control, mute state, captions availability, and progress without requiring a swipe gesture. Keyboard and switch users can move sequentially and trigger playback explicitly. Reduced motion removes snap animation where feasible, captions and audio descriptions remain selectable, and status updates avoid announcing every time tick.

Profile first play, gesture response, decoder count, memory, abandoned bytes, and failed play promises by device class. Roll out preload distance and player reuse independently so regressions can be attributed and disabled without changing feed identity.

Treat media policy as an adaptive client decision rather than one global preload count. A constrained phone may keep the active player, current poster, and one lightweight next candidate, while a capable device on a stable connection can prepare more. Capability evidence includes memory pressure, decoded-frame cost, connection changes, save-data preference, visibility, and recent swipe velocity. Adapt at safe boundaries so one card does not change quality repeatedly during playback. Record why a candidate was selected so field failures can be separated by format, device, and policy.

Player reuse also needs explicit hygiene. Before attaching the shared media element to a new item, pause the old source, detach item-specific listeners, invalidate the prior attempt, apply muted and captions preferences, set the new source, and handle the play promise. A late canplay, error, or play resolution from the old attempt is ignored. Posters keep fixed geometry throughout this handoff. This sequence prevents audio overlap, stale controls, decoder accumulation, and layout movement during rapid navigation.

Network adaptation should avoid reacting to one noisy sample. Use recent startup, rebuffer, throughput, and device evidence to adjust future candidates at item boundaries. Keep the user-selected captions, mute, and quality preference authoritative. If a lower-quality fallback is chosen, communicate only when that knowledge helps recovery; do not cover every card with transport detail. Test the policy with fast reverse swipes, orientation changes, Bluetooth interruptions, and data-saver transitions. After memory pressure, release inactive decoders and verify that current playback remains continuous.

blocks.title: endless short video feed answer rubric
items: Must — Keep a bounded active media window while preserving server item identity and cursor order.
Must — Pause playback and release expensive media resources when an item leaves the active slot.
Strong signal — Separate pagination acceptance from the visible projection and prefetch by user intent.
Strong signal — Restore position by stable item identity after refresh, insertion, or navigation.
Expert stretch — Adapt preload and rendition policy to network, memory, and reduced-motion signals.
Red flag — Starting playback for every mounted video or dropping accepted feed items to reduce render work.
